verdict.rationale: Across the whole Bible the figure named by H7854 "adversary" (satan), G1228 "slanderer" (diabolos), and G4567 "adversary, proper name" (satanas) consistently occupies the grammatical slot of a personal agent (someone who acts with intent). In Job 1 to 2 the adversary (satan) is the Subject of speech verbs, answers Yahweh with H6030 "to answer" (anah), and is addressed with H0559 "to say" (amar) plus H0413 "to, toward" (the directional preposition el) across nine verses. In Matthew 4, Mark 1 and 3, Luke 4, 10, 11 and 22, the figure approaches, stands, takes, shows, departs, and speaks, with verbs like G2476 "to stand" (histemi), G3880 "to take alongside" (paralambano), G1166 "to show" (deiknumi), G2980 "to speak" (laleo), G2036 "to say" (eipon) attaching to the named subject. John 8:44 predicates the personal-relational and moral nouns father, murderer, liar of him. 1 Peter 5:8 calls him "adversary, legal opponent" (antidikos) and seeking to devour. Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2 stack dragon, ancient serpent, "slanderer" (Diabolos), and "adversary" (Satanas) onto one referent who deceives and is bound. The personal-agent and opposer-of-God clauses hold across the whole Bible (pan-canonically, meaning spread across the whole Bible) with dense, recurring grammar. The created clause is not directly carried by these anchor word-stems, so it rests on inference from the wider canon and is recorded honestly as a residual.

scripture.force: The adversary (satan) comes among the sons of God to present himself before Yahweh. H0935 "to come" (bo), the verb of coming, takes the adversary (satan) as its personal subject, placing him as one acting agent within a council scene of agents rather than as an abstraction.

Yahweh says to the adversary (satan) using H0559 "to say" (amar) with the directional H0413 "to, toward" (el), and the adversary (satan) answers Yahweh using H6030 "to answer" (anah). Two-way address with a named respondent is grammar that requires a personal interlocutor (a personal conversation partner), not a force or principle. The same speech grammar continues in Job 1:8, Job 1:9, Job 1:12, Job 2:2, Job 2:3, Job 2:4, and Job 2:6.

Yahweh hands what Job has into the adversary's (satan's) hand, and the adversary (satan) then goes out from the presence of Yahweh, with H3318 "to go out" (yatsa). Possession of agency (the capacity to act on one's own), recipient of permission, and locomotion (physical movement from place to place) are predicated of the referent. These are agent attributes, not properties of a personification (a literary figure that gives human traits to a non-personal thing).

The adversary (satan) stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him, with H5975 "to stand" (amad) taking the adversary (satan) as Subject. Standing and accusing are agent verbs. The same accusatory frame recurs in Psalm 109:6 where an adversary (satan) is set against an enemy in a courtroom register (legal-courtroom style of language).

Adversary (satan), here for the first time without the article "the" (anarthrous, that is, without the Hebrew "the") in Hebrew narrative, stands up against Israel and incites David. The anarthrous (without "the") form moves the word toward a name rather than a title, and the verb of inciting H5496 "to incite" (suth) takes the adversary (satan) as personal subject acting upon a human king.

The tempter, "the one tempting" (ho peirazon), the participial designation (a noun-like phrase built on a verb) of the same figure introduced in verse 1 as "the slanderer" (ho diabolos), comes near and speaks, with "having come near" (proselthon) then "he said" (eipen). The pairing of approach and speech is the standard Greek frame for a personal speaker.

The "slanderer" (diabolos) takes Jesus to the holy city and stands him on the pinnacle, with G3880 "to take alongside" (paralambano) and G2476 "to stand" (histemi) as transitive verbs of physical action (verbs that act upon an object). A figurative or symbolic reading cannot account for these motion and placement verbs with a personal subject and a personal direct object.

The "slanderer" (diabolos) shows him all the kingdoms of the world, with G1166 "to show" (deiknumi) attaching to the personal subject. Show-and-tell predicates require an agent who can intend a display, which is the grammar of a personal being.

Jesus dismisses the figure with a vocative (the direct-address form of a noun), "Go away, Satan" (Hypage Satana), directly naming the same "slanderer" (diabolos) who has conducted the dialogue. A vocative (direct-address form) of direct address presupposes a personal addressee, and it equates the Greek "adversary" (Satanas) with the Hebrew adversary word-stem (satan) of Job and Zechariah.

Then the "slanderer" (diabolos) leaves him, "he leaves him" (aphiesin auton). The narrative records the agent departing, parallel to the adversary (satan) going out in Job 1:12. The structural rhyme across Testaments, present, dialogue, depart, confirms a personal subject in both.

"Adversary" (Satanas) asks for the disciples to sift them like wheat, with G1809 "to ask out, demand" (exaiteomai) the verb of formal request. To request is to intend, and to intend is to be a personal agent. The verb forecloses (rules out in advance) a non-personal reading.

The "slanderer" (diabolos) is called father, "father" (pater), and predicated as a murderer from the beginning, "man-killer from the beginning" (anthropoktonos ap arches), and a liar, "liar" (pseustes). Personal-relational and moral nouns are predicated of him, and the temporal phrase "from the beginning" attributes a continuous history of acting, which only fits a personal being with a will.

Believers are to stand, G2476 "to stand" (histemi), against the "schemes, planned tactics" (methodeiai) of the "slanderer" (diabolos). Schemes are intended, not random, and are predicated of a personal possessor by the possessive (genitive, the "of-X" grammatical form) "of the slanderer" (tou diabolou). "Scheme" (methodeia) is an agent noun for planned tactics.

The "slanderer" (diabolos) is your adversary, "legal opponent" (antidikos), prowling and seeking someone to devour. The legal-opponent noun "legal opponent" (antidikos) plus verbs of prowling and seeking describe purposeful hostile activity, the opposer element of the proposition. The lion image is a comparison, "as a lion" (hos leon), not an identity.

One referent is named four ways, the great dragon, the ancient serpent, "the one called slanderer" (ho kaloumenos Diabolos) and "the adversary" (ho Satanas), the one deceiving the whole world. The stacked appositional naming (where multiple names are placed side by side to refer to the same one) with the substantival participle "the one deceiving" (ho planon) unifies the Genesis 3 serpent and the named adversary as a single acting being who is cast out, "he was cast" (eblethe). Revelation 20:2 repeats this fourfold identification.

The serpent, "serpent" (nachash), is the Subject of the speech verb "to say" (amar) and conducts a multi-turn dialogue with the woman. The serpent speaks, reasons, and contradicts a divine command, which is agent grammar. The text here does not lexically equate the serpent (nachash) with the adversary (satan) word-stem, so the identification with the named adversary is supplied later in the canon at Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2.

complicating_texts.resolution: In Job and Zechariah the word-stem appears with the definite article "the", "the adversary" (ha-satan), which reads as a title or office, the accuser or adversary, rather than as a personal proper name. This qualifies the name claim. It does not, however, complicate personhood, because the same articular (with the article "the") form is the Subject of speech verbs, answers Yahweh, exercises a remit (an assigned scope of authority), and goes out, which are agent predicates. The article complicates onomastics (the study of names), not ontology (the question of what kind of being something is). By 1 Chronicles 21:1 the form is anarthrous (without the article "the"), and in the Greek New Testament the form "adversary" (Satanas) is fully a proper name.

In Numbers 22:22 and Numbers 22:32 the noun adversary (satan) is applied to the Angel of Yahweh as he stands in the way to oppose Balaam, and in 1 Samuel 29:4, 2 Samuel 19:22, and 1 Kings 11:14, 23, 25 it is applied to human opponents. This shows the word-stem has a common-noun sense, "an adversary", that is not always the named figure. So the noun alone does not prove the named figure, but in Job 1 to 2, Zechariah 3, 1 Chronicles 21, Psalm 109, and the unified New Testament usage with G1228 "slanderer" (diabolos) and G4567 "adversary" (satanas), the same word-stem is attached by context, definite article "the", and stacked New Testament naming to one specific opposing personal agent.

The Genesis 3 serpent is never lexically (in the actual words of the text) labeled "adversary" (satan) or "slanderer" (diabolos) within the Hebrew text of the passage, so reading the serpent as the personal adversary is a cross-canonical inference rather than a direct lexical datum (an item of evidence from the words themselves) at Genesis 3 itself. The link is supplied by Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2, which name the ancient serpent, "the ancient serpent" (ho ophis ho archaios), as "slanderer" (Diabolos) and "adversary" (Satanas) in the same noun phrase. Within Genesis 3 itself only the personal-agent grammar of the speaking serpent (nachash) is demonstrable.

The created element of the proposition, that this being is a creature with a beginning, is not carried by any anchor word-stem in this bundle. The texts establish a personal opposing agent across both Testaments with dense recurring grammar, but they do not lexically (in the actual words themselves) assert his origin as created. Resolving the created clause would require traversal to creation-of-spirits, angelic-origin, and fall-of-angels texts that were not supplied here. It is therefore left unresolved on the lexical (word-level) evidence at hand, flagged honestly, and does not subtract from the personal and opposing clauses.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied for the cited verses, and the bundle marks the question outside ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) scope. The four named figures in Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2, the dialogue frames in Matthew 4 and Luke 22:31, the predicates in John 8:44, and the council scene in Job 1 to 2 are textually stable in the supplied tradition. No plausible reading removes the personal agent.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Speech verbs, vocative (direct-address) address, multi-turn dialogue, possession, locomotion (physical movement), scheming, and accusing are all predicated of the referent across both Testaments. The grammar required by these predicates is the grammar of a personal being who intends, speaks, and moves.

The articular (with the article "the") Hebrew form "the adversary" (ha-satan) in Job 1 to 2 and Zechariah 3 supports reading adversary (satan) as a function word, "the accuser", in those passages, which qualifies the name claim. Personhood is left intact since the office is exercised by an acting subject who speaks and answers. The anarthrous (without the article "the") 1 Chronicles 21:1 and the Greek "adversary" (Satanas) as a proper name show progressive movement from office to name across the canon.

A reader could ask whether the dialogue scenes in Job 1 to 2 and Matthew 4 are dramatic personification (giving human traits to a non-personal thing) of an impersonal evil principle, the way wisdom is personified in Proverbs 8. The lexical (word-level) pattern resists this for three reasons named only from the words. First, the dialogues are multi-turn with two-way address and named vocatives (direct-address forms), not monologues praising an attribute. Second, the same figure crosses Testaments under multiple word-stems, "adversary" (satan), "slanderer" (diabolos), "adversary, proper name" (satanas), "serpent" (ophis), "dragon" (drakon), and these word-stems are stacked side by side (appositionally) in Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2 onto one referent. Third, the predicates include physical action verbs like G3880 "to take alongside" (paralambano), to take, and G1166 "to show" (deiknumi), to show, with personal direct objects, not the predicate types used for personified abstractions. The personification (figurative-human-trait) lens is therefore admissible as a question but is not sustainable as the dominant reading on this lexical (word-level) pattern.

Outside the named-figure passages the noun adversary (satan) is used of the Angel of Yahweh in Numbers 22 and of human opponents in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Kings, demonstrating a common-noun sense, "an adversary". This is real polysemy (the property of one word carrying multiple senses). It does not undercut the personal-being clause for the named figure, because in Job 1 to 2, Zechariah 3, 1 Chronicles 21:1, the New Testament use of G1228 "slanderer" (diabolos) and G4567 "adversary" (satanas), and the Revelation 12:9 stack, context, articulation (presence or absence of "the"), and discourse role isolate the specific personal adversary.

hermeneutics.notes: The serpent of Genesis 3 and the named adversary are joined by analogia scripturae (the principle of reading Scripture in light of Scripture) through the side-by-side (appositional) naming in Revelation 12:9 and Revelation 20:2. The move from articular (with "the") "the adversary" (ha-satan) in the older texts to the anarthrous (without "the") proper name "adversary" (Satanas) in the Greek reflects progressive disclosure (the gradual unveiling of truth across the canon) of the same figure rather than two different figures.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What does the canon say about the referent named by the word-stems adversary (satan) and slanderer (diabolos), regarding whether it acts as a personal agent (someone who acts with intent), whether it opposes God and his people, and whether it is presented as a created spiritual being.
stem_audit.notes: The stem bundles three claims, personal, created, and opposing, and treats the created clause as settled. The lexical (word-level) bundle strongly supports the personal and opposing clauses, with dense pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) grammar, but does not directly witness the created clause, since no creation-of-spirits or angelic-origin word-stem was supplied. The verdict is derived on the original stem, and the gap on the created clause is recorded honestly in complicating_texts and rationale rather than smuggled past.

lay_summary: The question asks whether Satan is a real, personal, created spiritual being who opposes God and his people. Looking only at the original-language words, the picture is consistent. The Hebrew word "adversary" (satan), H7854, the Greek words "slanderer" (diabolos), G1228, and "adversary" (Satanas), G4567, attach to a figure who behaves like a person. In Job chapter 1 and 2 this figure comes into a gathering, is spoken to by Yahweh, and answers back across nine consecutive verses. The verbs of speaking and answering require someone who can be addressed and can reply. In Matthew chapter 4 the same figure approaches, speaks several times, takes Jesus to different places, shows him kingdoms, and finally departs, and Jesus turns and addresses him directly by name as Satan. Direct address by name only works toward a person, and physical-motion verbs like take and show point to an agent who intends an act. John chapter 8 calls him a father, a murderer from the beginning, and a liar, descriptions of a being with a will and a history. Luke chapter 22 has him asking to sift the disciples, which is a formal request that only a person can make. Ephesians chapter 6 has him owning schemes. First Peter chapter 5 names him an adversary who prowls and seeks someone to devour, and the roaring lion is a comparison there, not his nature. Revelation chapter 12 and chapter 20 gather four labels onto one figure, the dragon, the ancient serpent, the Devil, and Satan, the one who deceives the whole world, and this is what links the speaking serpent (nachash) of Genesis chapter 3 to the named adversary. Two honest limits remain. In Job and Zechariah the word carries the article "the", "the adversary" (ha-satan), which can read as a title, the accuser, though the same figure still speaks and acts as a person, and by First Chronicles 21 and in the New Testament the form is a proper name. And the word created is not proven by these particular texts, since none of the supplied words address his origin. So the words strongly support a real, personal, opposing being. The created part rests on wider teaching not contained in this set of texts and is flagged.
